questions.stem: When does a charged particle feel a force in a magnetic field?

options.text: when it moves across the field lines instead of running along them
options.explanation: Both conditions — motion and a cross-field component — are required.

options.text: whenever it is inside the field, moving or not
options.explanation: A stationary charge feels no magnetic force.

options.text: only when it moves parallel to the field
options.explanation: Parallel motion is exactly the zero-force case.

options.text: only when the field is switched off
options.explanation: The force exists because of the field, not its absence.

questions.stem: An electron travels along the magnetic field lines, never crossing them. What force does it feel?

options.text: a force that slows the electron
options.explanation: The magnetic force never slows a charge to zero like this.

options.text: zero
options.explanation: Motion parallel to the field produces no magnetic force.

options.text: maximum force along the field
options.explanation: Force acts across the field, and parallel motion cancels it entirely.

options.text: a sideways force into the page
options.explanation: No component across the field means no sideways push.

questions.stem: The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field is greatest when the motion is:

options.text: at 45 degrees to the field lines
options.explanation: 45 degrees gives a partial force, less than the perpendicular maximum.

options.text: opposite to the field direction
options.explanation: Anti-parallel is still parallel — zero force.

options.text: perpendicular to the field lines
options.explanation: Perpendicular motion gives the full cross-field interaction.

options.text: parallel to the field lines
options.explanation: Parallel gives zero, the minimum not the maximum.

questions.stem: A proton and an electron enter the same field with the same velocity, both moving across the field lines. How do their deflections compare?

options.text: they deflect the same way
options.explanation: Opposite charges feel opposite force directions.

options.text: neither deflects
options.explanation: Cross-field motion gives both a force.

options.text: only the proton deflects
options.explanation: Both charged particles feel the field's force.

options.text: they deflect towards opposite sides
options.explanation: The force direction follows the charge sign, so the two bend apart.

questions.stem: What does the magnetic force do to the SPEED of a deflected electron?

options.text: the speed stays the same; only the direction changes
options.explanation: The force acts at right angles to the motion, steering without speeding.

options.text: the speed increases as it bends
options.explanation: A perpendicular force cannot push the particle faster along its path.

options.text: the speed decreases to zero
options.explanation: Nothing in the magnetic interaction stops the particle.

options.text: the speed first rises then falls
options.explanation: Speed is untouched throughout the deflection.

questions.stem: State the two conditions needed for a charged particle to experience a force in a magnetic field.
questions.modelAnswer: The particle must be moving, and its motion must not be parallel to the magnetic field lines.

questions.stem: State the direction of the force on a moving charge relative to the field and the motion.
questions.modelAnswer: The force is at right angles to both the velocity and the magnetic field lines.

questions.stem: Explain why an electron moving exactly along a field line experiences no magnetic force.
questions.modelAnswer: The magnetic force on a charge depends on the component of its motion across the field lines. Motion exactly parallel to the field has no cross-field component, so the field cannot exert any sideways push; the electron simply continues undeflected along the line.

questions.stem: In a laboratory tube, a beam of electrons fires across a magnetic field at right angles. Describe and explain what an observer sees.
questions.modelAnswer: The beam bends into a curve as it crosses the field, because each electron feels a force at right angles to its motion. The deflection is sideways — perpendicular to both the beam and the field — and reverses side if the field direction or the beam current is reversed.
